course.title: World History
course.description: A global tour of the human past — from the first farming villages and river-valley cities to classical empires, world religions, trade networks, the Islamic golden age, and the first age of global contact. Structure adapted from OpenStax World History (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: The Neolithic Revolution refers to…
options: the shift from foraging to farming and settled villages
questions.explanation: Around 10,000 BCE humans in several regions began domesticating plants and animals — see 'Early societies'.

questions.prompt: Cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems, was developed by the…
questions.explanation: Sumerians pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay along the Tigris and Euphrates — see 'River-valley civilizations'.

questions.prompt: The Achaemenid Persian Empire was founded by…
questions.explanation: Cyrus the Great united the Persians and Medes in the 6th century BCE — see 'Classical empires'.

questions.prompt: The Silk Road primarily connected…
options: East Asia and the Mediterranean world
questions.explanation: Overland routes linked Han China to Rome through Central Asia — see 'Trade networks'.

questions.prompt: The House of Wisdom, a famous center of translation and scholarship, was located in…
questions.explanation: The Abbasid caliphs sponsored it in Baghdad — see 'Islamic golden age'.

questions.prompt: Mansa Musa, renowned for his wealth and pilgrimage, ruled the empire of…
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa of Mali controlled West African gold and salt trade — see 'The medieval world'.

questions.prompt: The 'Columbian Exchange' describes…
options: a treaty between Spain and Portugal
the transfer of crops, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia
questions.explanation: After 1492, biological and cultural transfers reshaped both hemispheres — see 'Global contact'.

questions.prompt: The great treasure-fleet voyages of the early 1400s were led by Admiral Zheng He for the…
questions.explanation: Ming China launched vast voyages across the Indian Ocean decades before Columbus — see 'Global contact'.

lessons.title: Early societies and the river-valley civilizations
lessons.grammar_note: Chronology cue: 'BCE' counts down toward year 1, 'CE' counts up. 3000 BCE is older than 500 BCE.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the Neolithic Revolution and name the major river-valley civilizations. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what change does the word *Neolithic* mark in how people got their food?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For most of the human story, people foraged in small mobile bands. Beginning around 10,000 BCE — independently in several places — communities learned to farm and herd. This *Neolithic Revolution* produced food surpluses, which let populations grow, settle, and specialize. Where large rivers flooded predictably and left rich soil, the first cities appeared: Sumer on the Tigris and Euphrates, Egypt on the Nile, the Harappan culture on the Indus, and Shang society on the Yellow River. Surplus fed rulers, priests, artisans, and soldiers, and record-keeping produced early writing such as *cuneiform* and Egyptian hieroglyphs.

sections.heading: Reading the evidence
sections.text: Historians infer these societies from their remains. The grid-planned streets and covered drains of Mohenjo-daro on the Indus suggest careful civic planning, even though we still cannot fully read Harappan script. Clay cuneiform tablets from Sumer record grain and beer rations — proof that writing began largely as accounting before it recorded stories like the Epic of Gilgamesh.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each civilization to its river: (1) Egypt, (2) Sumer, (3) Harappan, (4) Shang. Rivers: Indus / Nile / Yellow / Tigris-Euphrates. Answers: 1-Nile, 2-Tigris-Euphrates, 3-Indus, 4-Yellow. Bonus: name one thing food surplus made possible. Answer: cities, specialized jobs, or writing (any one).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking farming was invented once and spread everywhere — it arose independently in Southwest Asia, China, the Americas, and elsewhere. Mistake: assuming writing began as literature — it began as record-keeping. Exit: (a) What did food surplus allow? (b) Which Mesopotamian people used cuneiform? Answers: settled cities and specialized labor; the Sumerians.

lessons.title: Classical empires: Persia, India, Han China, and Rome
lessons.grammar_note: An *empire* rules many peoples under one authority — watch for how each solved the same problem: governing distance.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compare how four classical empires held together vast territory. Warm-up: who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Between roughly 550 BCE and 500 CE, several large empires rose on different continents and faced the same challenge: ruling millions across great distances. *Achaemenid Persia* (founded by Cyrus the Great, expanded by Darius I) divided its lands into provinces called *satrapies* linked by the Royal Road. In South Asia, the *Maurya* Empire — whose emperor Ashoka promoted Buddhist ideals after a bloody war — and later the *Gupta* rulers unified much of India. *Han China* governed through a trained bureaucracy shaped by Confucian ideas. *Rome* grew from a republic into an empire ringing the Mediterranean, binding it with roads, law, and citizenship.

sections.heading: Source reasoning
sections.text: Ashoka left his policies carved on stone pillars across India, publicly urging tolerance and welfare — one of history's earliest state propaganda campaigns preserved in the ruler's own words. Compare this to Rome's roads or Persia's Royal Road: each empire advertised and enforced its power through infrastructure that also sped armies, messages, and taxes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match ruler or feature to empire: (1) Cyrus the Great, (2) Ashoka's pillars, (3) Confucian bureaucracy, (4) Mediterranean-wide citizenship. Empires: Rome / Han China / Persia / Maurya India. Answers: 1-Persia, 2-Maurya India, 3-Han China, 4-Rome. Bonus: name one tool many empires used to govern distance. Answer: roads (also bureaucracy, common law, or coinage).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating Rome as the only 'classical' empire — Han China governed a comparable population at the same time. Mistake: confusing the Maurya and Gupta as one dynasty; they are centuries apart. Exit: (a) What were Persian provinces called? (b) Which empire relied on a Confucian-trained bureaucracy? Answers: satrapies; Han China.

lessons.title: World religions and the Silk Road
lessons.grammar_note: Trade networks moved goods AND ideas — when you read 'Silk Road', think 'highway for religions and disease too'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how long-distance trade spread religions and connected distant societies. Warm-up: which two ends of Eurasia did the Silk Road link?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: As empires stabilized, merchants stitched Eurasia and Africa together. The overland *Silk Road* carried Chinese silk, Central Asian horses, and Roman glass between East Asia and the Mediterranean, while *Indian Ocean* sailors rode seasonal *monsoon* winds between East Africa, Arabia, India, and Southeast Asia. These routes moved more than goods: *Buddhism* traveled from India into Central Asia and China; *Christianity* spread across the Roman world and into Africa and Asia; and Hindu and Confucian ideas moved with traders and pilgrims. Belief systems that offered universal messages — open to anyone, not just one people — spread especially fast along these networks.

sections.heading: Source reasoning
sections.text: Cave monasteries at Dunhuang, a Silk Road oasis in western China, are packed with Buddhist paintings and one of the world's oldest printed books, the Diamond Sutra (868 CE). Their location — a trade crossroads, not the religion's Indian homeland — shows how faith rode commerce far from where it began. The same routes later carried the plague, a reminder that connection cuts both ways.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: True or false, with a reason: (1) The Silk Road moved only physical goods. (2) Buddhism began in India but spread to China. (3) Indian Ocean trade depended on monsoon winds. (4) Universal religions spread more easily along trade routes. Answers: (1) False — it moved ideas, religions, and disease; (2) True; (3) True — sailors timed voyages to the winds; (4) True.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: picturing one paved road — the Silk Road was a shifting web of routes, most goods changing hands many times. Mistake: thinking religions spread only by conquest; merchants and pilgrims mattered as much. Exit: (a) What winds powered Indian Ocean trade? (b) Name one religion that spread along the Silk Road. Answers: the monsoons; Buddhism (also Christianity or Islam).

questions.prompt: The Neolithic Revolution most directly produced…
questions.explanation: Farming surpluses enabled cities and specialization.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of civilization and river is correct?
questions.explanation: The Harappan culture developed along the Indus.

questions.prompt: Persian provinces governed by appointed officials were called…
questions.explanation: Satraps ruled satrapies, linked by the Royal Road.

questions.prompt: Ashoka, who spread Buddhist ideals through carved edicts, ruled which empire?
questions.explanation: Ashoka was a Maurya emperor of India.

questions.prompt: Indian Ocean trade voyages were timed to…
questions.explanation: Monsoons reversed direction with the seasons, guiding sailors.

questions.prompt: Besides goods, the Silk Road is famous for spreading…
options: the printing press to Europe first
questions.explanation: Ideas, faiths, and pathogens all traveled the routes.

lessons.title: The medieval world and the Islamic golden age
lessons.grammar_note: 'Medieval' means 'middle age' (roughly 500–1500 CE) — but it was a global era, not just a European one.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe key centers of learning and power across the medieval world. Warm-up: in which city did Abbasid caliphs sponsor the House of Wisdom?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The centuries after 500 CE were a vibrant, connected age far beyond Europe. Under the *Abbasid Caliphate*, Baghdad's *House of Wisdom* gathered scholars who translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works and pushed knowledge forward: al-Khwarizmi's writing gave us the word *algebra*, and Ibn Sina's medical texts were studied for centuries. In West Africa, the empires of Ghana, *Mali*, and Songhai grew rich on gold and salt; Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made *Timbuktu* a hub of scholarship. *Tang and Song China* invented printing, paper money, and gunpowder. Meanwhile the *Mongol* conquests briefly united much of Eurasia, and the resulting 'Pax Mongolica' made long-distance travel safer than ever.

sections.heading: Source reasoning
sections.text: When Mansa Musa passed through Cairo on pilgrimage in 1324, chroniclers reported he gave away so much gold that its value there dropped for years. Whether or not the figures are exact, the story — recorded by writers far from Mali — is evidence of how West African wealth impressed the wider Islamic world, and of how much trade linked the Sahara to the Mediterranean.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match achievement to place: (1) House of Wisdom / algebra, (2) gold-salt trade and Timbuktu, (3) printing and gunpowder, (4) Pax Mongolica overland safety. Places: Song China / Mali / Abbasid Baghdad / Mongol Empire. Answers: 1-Abbasid Baghdad, 2-Mali, 3-Song China, 4-Mongol Empire. Bonus: which word comes from an Arabic mathematical text? Answer: algebra.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling this era the 'Dark Ages' — outside western Europe, Baghdad, Timbuktu, and Kaifeng were flourishing. Mistake: assuming gunpowder was a European invention; it came from China. Exit: (a) Which West African ruler is famous for his pilgrimage and gold? (b) Name one Chinese invention of this period. Answers: Mansa Musa of Mali; printing, paper money, or gunpowder.

lessons.title: The age of exploration and global contact
lessons.grammar_note: 'Discovery' is a matter of perspective — lands were 'new' only to the newcomers. Prefer 'contact' or 'encounter'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how the world's hemispheres became linked after 1400 and weigh the consequences. Warm-up: which Chinese admiral led huge fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Long-distance exploration was not only European. In 1405–1433 the Ming admiral *Zheng He* commanded fleets of hundreds of ships as far as East Africa. Soon after, Portuguese and Spanish voyages sought sea routes to Asian trade — and in 1492 an expedition led by Columbus reached the Americas, where the *Aztec* and *Inca* empires already ruled millions. The linking of the hemispheres set off the *Columbian Exchange*: maize, potatoes, and tomatoes spread to Afro-Eurasia, while wheat, horses, and cattle crossed to the Americas. But the exchange also carried diseases like smallpox, which killed a huge share of Indigenous Americans, and it fed a brutal transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans.

sections.heading: Source reasoning
sections.text: Spanish accounts marveled at the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan — a lake city with causeways and markets they compared to the greatest cities of Europe. Reading such sources critically means noting both what they reveal (the sophistication of American societies) and their bias (written by conquerors justifying conquest). The catastrophic population collapse that followed was driven less by battle than by imported disease.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Sort each item — 'to the Americas' or 'to Afro-Eurasia': (1) potatoes, (2) horses, (3) maize, (4) smallpox, (5) tomatoes, (6) wheat. Answers: to the Americas — horses, smallpox, wheat; to Afro-Eurasia — potatoes, maize, tomatoes. Bonus: name the American empire centered on Tenochtitlan. Answer: the Aztec (Mexica) Empire.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking exploration began with Europe — Zheng He's fleets predate Columbus by decades. Mistake: imagining the Americas were empty; the Aztec and Inca ruled vast, complex states. Exit: (a) What was the single biggest cause of Indigenous population loss? (b) Name one crop the Americas gave the world. Answers: imported disease such as smallpox; potatoes, maize, or tomatoes.

lessons.title: Applied project: make a historical argument

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Write a short, evidence-based argument answering ONE of these questions: (a) Which connected the world's peoples more powerfully — the Silk Road or the Columbian Exchange? (b) Was the medieval period better described as a 'dark age' or a 'golden age', and for whom? You are making a case, not just summarizing.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State a clear thesis — a sentence someone could reasonably disagree with. 2) Give at least three pieces of specific evidence from the course (people, places, dates, or exchanges). 3) Address one counterargument fairly, then explain why your position still holds. 4) Make sure your evidence is globally balanced — draw on more than one region.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Thesis is arguable, not a bare fact. ✔ At least three concrete, accurate examples support it. ✔ You engaged a real counterargument instead of a strawman. ✔ Your evidence spans multiple world regions, not just Europe. If all four are true, you've argued like a historian.
